label: Large Sample Asymptotic Theory
notes: We open the chapter by fixing the asymptotic regime: a growing sample of orientations drawn from a distribution on a special manifold. The central question is how an estimator of the modal orientation and concentration behaves as the sample size diverges, and where on the manifold its fluctuations should be measured.

label: The Estimation Problem
notes: Here we name the objects: a population distribution on a Stiefel or Grassmann manifold, a true modal orientation, a concentration parameter, and a maximum likelihood estimator built from independent draws. Fixing this notation early lets every later asymptotic statement attach cleanly to a concrete parameter and a concrete estimator.

label: Consistency of the MLE
notes: Consistency is the first guarantee: as the sample grows the estimator settles onto the true parameter. We sketch the argument through uniform convergence of the normalized log-likelihood and a well separated maximum, so the maximizer of the sample objective converges to the maximizer of its expectation.

label: Tangent Space at the Mode
notes: Because the manifold is curved, fluctuations cannot live in a flat parameter vector. We linearize at the modal point and pass to its tangent space, the natural flat arena where small deviations add like vectors. The exponential map carries these tangent vectors back onto the manifold near the mode.

label: Asymptotic Normality
notes: This is the central limit statement for manifold estimators. Rescaled by the square root of the sample size, the tangent coordinate of the estimator converges to a centered Gaussian. The curvature enters only through the choice of chart, while the limiting law itself is an ordinary multivariate normal on the tangent space.

label: Fisher Information
notes: The Fisher information matrix quantifies how sharply the likelihood distinguishes nearby parameters along tangent directions. Computed as the expected outer product of the score, it sets the curvature of the expected log-likelihood at the mode and becomes the precision matrix of the limiting Gaussian distribution we derived.

label: Asymptotic Covariance
notes: Asymptotic efficiency closes the loop: the limiting covariance of the estimator is the inverse Fisher information scaled by one over the sample size. Larger information yields a tighter limit, and the inverse directly predicts the size and shape of the confidence ellipse drawn in the tangent space.

label: Concentration of the Sampling Law
notes: Visually, increasing the sample size shrinks the sampling distribution toward the true parameter. The confidence ellipse contracts at the parametric root-n rate, its axes governed by the inverse information eigenvalues. We watch three sample sizes nest inside one another around the modal point.

label: Estimating Concentration
notes: Beyond orientation we estimate concentration. Its score and information decouple partially from the orientation block, and its maximum likelihood estimator inherits the same root-n normal behavior. We note how strong concentration sharpens orientation information, coupling the two limiting variances through the population law.

label: CLT for the Mean Matrix
notes: The sample mean matrix is the workhorse statistic. A matrix central limit theorem shows its entries, recentered and rescaled, converge jointly to a Gaussian array whose covariance reflects the population second moments. Projecting this limit onto the tangent space recovers the estimator's asymptotic normality.

label: Worked Asymptotic Check
notes: We run a finite computation that mirrors the notebook: draw points near a mode, form the sample mean direction, and compare the empirical fluctuation scale against the predicted inverse-information envelope. The diagnostic should stay finite and shrink at the root-n rate as the sample grows.

label: Summary and Outlook
notes: We close by collecting the asymptotic toolkit: consistency, tangent-space normality, Fisher information, and the inverse-information covariance. These results turn manifold estimators into objects with ordinary Gaussian limits, enabling confidence regions and tests that later chapters refine for hypothesis problems on special manifolds.
